description: Heart structure, the pathway of blood, blood vessels and how the cardiovascular system responds to exercise.
content_html:
The Heart: Structure and Function

The heart is a hollow, muscular organ roughly the size of a fist, located in the chest slightly left of centre behind the sternum. It is divided into four chambers by a central wall called the septum. The two upper chambers are called atria (singular: atrium) — the right atrium receives deoxygenated blood returning from the body, and the left atrium receives oxygenated blood returning from the lungs. The two lower chambers are called ventricles — the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs, and the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood to the rest of the body. The left ventricle has a thicker, more muscular wall than the right because it must generate much higher pressure to push blood all the way around the body.

Valves inside the heart open due to changes in blood pressure and close automatically to prevent backflow of blood. The right side of the heart and the left side each have valves between the atrium and the ventricle (atrioventricular valves) and between the ventricle and the outgoing vessel (semilunar valves). You do not need to name individual valves, but you must know they prevent backflow.

The Cardiac Cycle: How the Heart Beats

The heart works through a two-phase cycle. During diastole, the chambers relax and fill with blood — the atria fill with incoming blood and then push it through to the ventricles. During systole, the ventricles contract and eject blood out of the heart: the right ventricle forces blood into the pulmonary artery (to the lungs) and the left ventricle forces blood into the aorta (to the body). This cycle repeats every beat, which at rest typically occurs 60–80 times per minute.

The Pathway of Blood Through the Heart and Lungs

Following the pathway of blood precisely is a common exam demand. Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium via the vena cava. From the right atrium it passes through a valve into the right ventricle. The right ventricle then contracts and forces the blood through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. In the lungs, carbon dioxide is released and oxygen is picked up by haemoglobin in the red blood cells to form oxyhaemoglobin. The now-oxygenated blood returns to the heart via the pulmonary vein, entering the left atrium. It passes through a valve into the left ventricle, which contracts powerfully and ejects the oxygenated blood into the aorta — from which it is distributed to every organ and muscle in the body.

Key Fact

Blood pathway: vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs (gas exchange) → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body. Note that the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood — this is the opposite of most arteries.

Blood Vessels: Arteries, Veins and Capillaries

Arteries carry blood away from the heart. They have thick, muscular walls because they must withstand the high pressure generated by the ventricular contraction. The walls are elastic, allowing them to stretch and recoil with each heartbeat, smoothing out the pulsed blood flow. All arteries (except the pulmonary artery) carry oxygenated blood.

Veins carry blood back towards the heart. They have thinner walls than arteries because blood pressure is much lower by the time it reaches the venous system. Veins contain valves that prevent backflow, which is especially important in the legs where blood must travel upward against gravity. All veins (except the pulmonary vein) carry deoxygenated blood.

Capillaries are the microscopic vessels that form the link between arteries and veins in the tissues. Their walls are just one cell thick, allowing oxygen and nutrients to diffuse into the muscle cells and carbon dioxide and waste products to diffuse back into the blood. Every working muscle is surrounded by a dense network of capillaries. Long-term aerobic training increases capillary density in muscles, improving oxygen delivery.

During exercise, the working muscles need much more oxygen and glucose than at rest. The body redirects blood flow using two mechanisms. Vasoconstriction reduces the diameter of blood vessels supplying areas that are not active during exercise (e.g. the digestive system), reducing blood flow to those areas. Vasodilation increases the diameter of the blood vessels supplying the active muscles, dramatically increasing blood flow to where it is needed most. The redistribution of blood during exercise through vasoconstriction and vasodilation is called the ‘vascular shunt’. This is why it is inadvisable to exercise vigorously immediately after a large meal — the digestive system is competing with muscles for blood supply.

Cardiac Output, Stroke Volume and Heart Rate

Three linked measurements describe how efficiently the heart pumps blood. Stroke volume is the amount of blood pumped out of the heart with each beat. At rest, stroke volume is approximately 70 ml. Heart rate is the number of beats per minute (bpm). A typical resting heart rate is 60–80 bpm (trained endurance athletes may have a resting heart rate as low as 40 bpm — a long-term adaptation called bradycardia). Cardiac output (Q) is the product of the two:

$$Q = \text{stroke volume} \times \text{heart rate}$$

At rest: Q = 70 ml × 72 bpm = 5,040 ml/min (approximately 5 litres per minute). During intense exercise, heart rate can rise to 200 bpm or more and stroke volume increases to around 110–130 ml, so cardiac output can reach 20–25 litres per minute in a trained athlete.

Key Fact

Cardiac output (Q) = stroke volume × heart rate. Always show the formula, substitute the values, and include the unit (ml/min or L/min). Example: Q = 70 ml × 72 bpm = 5,040 ml/min. At maximum exercise this can rise to over 20,000 ml/min in a trained athlete.

A heart rate graph during exercise typically shows four phases. First, an anticipatory rise — heart rate climbs before exercise even begins, driven by the release of adrenaline as the performer prepares mentally and physically. This is why athletes’ hearts are already beating faster as they stand in the starting blocks. Second, heart rate rises steeply at the onset of exercise as oxygen demand increases. Third, a plateau occurs at a steady exercise intensity as supply and demand equalise. Fourth, a recovery curve drops steeply at first then more gradually after exercise stops, as the body repays its oxygen debt. A trained performer recovers faster (steeper drop) because their cardiovascular system is more efficient.
exam_tip_html: The cardiac output calculation is one of the most predictable questions in this unit — always worth attempting. Show three things: (1) the formula (Q = stroke volume × heart rate), (2) the substitution with figures from the question, and (3) the answer with the correct unit (ml/min or L/min). Missing the unit is a frequent error that costs the final mark. On a ‘Describe the pathway of blood’ question, a common mistake is to say the pulmonary artery carries oxygenated blood — it is the one artery in the body that carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs. For extended-response questions on the cardiovascular system, link vasoconstriction and vasodilation explicitly to the redistribution of blood to working muscles, and give a sport-specific example of why this matters.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Blood pathway through the heart: vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood — this is the exception to the rule that arteries carry oxygenated blood.
  • Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate (Q = SV × HR). At rest this is approximately 5 litres per minute; during maximal exercise it can exceed 20 litres per minute in a trained athlete.
  • Vasodilation increases blood flow to working muscles during exercise; vasoconstriction reduces blood flow to inactive areas. Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure; veins return blood to the heart under low pressure; capillaries allow gas and nutrient exchange with tissues.

practice_questions.text: Name the vessel that carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
During a 5 km race, a runner has a heart rate of 160 bpm and a stroke volume of 95 ml. Calculate her cardiac output. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct formula and substitution: Q = stroke volume × heart rate = 95 ml × 160 bpm; 1 mark for correct answer with unit: 15,200 ml/min (or 15.2 L/min). If the answer is correct but the unit is missing, award 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: Describe the structure of arteries and explain how this structure relates to their function.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that arteries have thick, muscular and elastic walls; 1 mark for explaining that thick walls are needed to withstand the high pressure generated by the ventricle contracting; 1 mark for explaining that elastic walls allow the vessel to stretch and recoil with each heartbeat, smoothing blood flow and helping maintain pressure between beats.

practice_questions.text: Explain how vasoconstriction and vasodilation work together to meet the increased oxygen demands of working muscles during a sprint.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining vasodilation: the widening of blood vessels supplying the active muscles, increasing blood flow; 1 mark for defining vasoconstriction: the narrowing of blood vessels supplying inactive areas (e.g. digestive system, skin), reducing blood flow there; 1 mark for explaining that this redistribution channels more blood (and therefore oxygen) to the working muscles; 1 mark for applying to sprinting (e.g. the leg muscles receive a much greater share of the total cardiac output during a sprint, meeting the high ATP demand for explosive contraction).

practice_questions.text: Table 1 shows data for a trained cyclist at rest and during a 20-minute time trial. Resting: heart rate 48 bpm, stroke volume 85 ml. During time trial: heart rate 172 bpm, stroke volume 115 ml. Calculate the cardiac output at rest and during the time trial, and interpret what the data tells you about the physiological demands of a cycling time trial.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct resting cardiac output: 48 × 85 = 4,080 ml/min; 1 mark for correct exercise cardiac output: 172 × 115 = 19,780 ml/min; 1 mark for a valid comparison using both figures (e.g. cardiac output increases by approximately 15,700 ml/min during the time trial — almost five times the resting value); 1 mark for an explanation of the sporting implication (e.g. the dramatic increase in cardiac output reflects the greatly elevated oxygen demand of the working leg muscles during sustained high-intensity cycling; the trained athlete’s low resting heart rate and high stroke volume indicate a strong, efficient heart capable of meeting this demand). If calculations are incorrect but method is sound, award 1 mark for working and 1 mark for a valid interpretation of their calculated figures.

practice_questions.text: A weekend footballer is considering whether to add cardiovascular training to his programme. Evaluate the importance of the cardiovascular system to his performance in a 90-minute match, using your knowledge of heart structure, blood vessels and the responses to exercise.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of content covered with accuracy — heart chambers and their roles, cardiac output calculation applied to exercise demand, blood vessel functions, vasoconstriction/vasodilation, anticipatory rise and recovery curve; all applied specifically and consistently to a 90-minute football match; balanced evaluation (importance acknowledged with detail, plus limitations or individual variation considered); clear justified conclusion.

Secure: Most cardiovascular structures and responses covered with reasonable accuracy; applied to football; conclusion reached; some minor inaccuracies or undeveloped points.

Developing: Cardiovascular system described with limited application to football; cardiac output mentioned but may not be calculated; one-sided (either all positive or missing evaluation of how CV fitness affects football performance).

Emerging: Basic points about heart rate increasing during exercise; limited structure or sporting application.

Content pointers: heart rate rises from resting ~72 bpm to 170–185 bpm during high-intensity phases; cardiac output increases from ~5 L/min at rest to over 20 L/min during sprints; vasodilation delivers more oxygen to the leg and core muscles during attacking runs; vasoconstriction reduces blood supply to non-essential organs; capillary networks in working muscles allow gas exchange; a high stroke volume (trained heart) means the footballer’s heart does not have to beat as fast to deliver the same cardiac output, delaying fatigue; a trained CV system also supports faster recovery between high-intensity sprints within the match.

knowledge_checks.q: Which vessel carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs?
What is the formula for cardiac output?
options: Cardiac output = heart rate + stroke volume
Cardiac output = stroke volume ÷ heart rate
Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate
Cardiac output = heart rate ÷ stroke volume

knowledge_checks.q: The _____ is the muscular wall that divides the left and right sides of the heart.
During exercise, _____ widens blood vessels supplying the working muscles to increase blood flow.
Match each blood vessel to its description:
right: Carry blood away from the heart under high pressure
Return blood to the heart; contain valves to prevent backflow
One-cell-thick vessels allowing gas exchange with tissues

flashcard_questions.q: What does the septum do in the heart?
flashcard_questions.a: Divides the left and right sides, preventing oxygenated and deoxygenated blood from mixing.

flashcard_questions.q: Which vessel carries deoxygenated blood FROM the right ventricle TO the lungs?
Which vessel carries oxygenated blood FROM the lungs TO the left atrium?
Which large vessel carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body?
Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate. What is the unit?

flashcard_questions.a: The volume of blood ejected by one ventricle per heartbeat (in ml).

flashcard_questions.q: Calculate cardiac output: stroke volume 70 ml, heart rate 72 bpm.
What is an anticipatory rise in heart rate?
flashcard_questions.a: Heart rate increases before exercise begins, triggered by adrenaline release.

flashcard_questions.q: What is vasodilation and when does it occur during exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: Widening of blood vessels to working muscles, increasing blood flow during exercise.

flashcard_questions.q: What is vasoconstriction and where does it occur during exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: Narrowing of vessels to inactive areas (e.g. digestive system), reducing blood flow there.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do arteries have thick, elastic walls?
flashcard_questions.a: To withstand and smooth out the high-pressure pulse of blood from the ventricle.
To prevent backflow of blood, especially in the legs where blood flows against gravity.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are capillary walls only one cell thick?
flashcard_questions.a: To allow rapid diffusion of oxygen and nutrients into tissues and CO2 out.

flashcard_questions.q: The vena cava carries blood into which chamber of the heart?

glossary_terms.definition: The muscular wall that divides the left and right sides of the heart, preventing oxygenated and deoxygenated blood from mixing.
The large vein that returns deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium of the heart.
The vessel carrying deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs for gas exchange.
The vessel that carries oxygenated blood from the lungs back to the left atrium of the heart.
The largest artery in the body, carrying oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the rest of the body.
The narrowing of a blood vessel, reducing blood flow to that area.
The widening of a blood vessel, increasing blood flow to that area.
The volume of blood ejected by one ventricle in a single heartbeat, measured in millilitres (ml).
The number of times the heart beats per minute (bpm).
The total volume of blood pumped by one ventricle per minute; calculated as stroke volume multiplied by heart rate.
Thick-walled, elastic blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart under high pressure.
Thin-walled blood vessels with valves that carry blood back towards the heart under low pressure.
Microscopic, single-cell-thick blood vessels that link arteries to veins and allow gas and nutrient exchange with body tissues.
